t: unblemished. Whole, without a bodily defect.
and choice. See below 2:8, 7:1-2.
by oral tradition. Tradition of the Sages.

even if he consecrated it for the value of libations. Not so that the animal be offered on the altar, but so that libations be bought with the proceeds of its sale and those be offered on the altar; but it is permitted to consecrate it for the Temple repair fund so that things not offered on the altar be bought with its proceeds (Bavli Temurah 7b).

one who intended to say shelamim and said olah. He wanted to consecrate an animal as a peace offering, and when he actually consecrated it he mistakenly said it should be an olah (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:12).
he has said nothing. And the animal is not sacred.
until his mouth and heart are equal. That there be agreement between his speech and his thought.
even though he intended a forbidden act. Of consecrating a blemished animal for the altar.
he is not flogged. Since the sanctity did not take effect.
who thought. Who supposed.
it is sacred. Even though he did it because he did not know that it was forbidden, it is not considered a consecration in error, for he did intend to consecrate.
and he is not flogged. Because the matter was done unintentionally.
the portions of blemished animals meant for the altar. The fats and other organs that are burned on the altar.
with a permanent blemish or a transient blemish. A transient blemish is one that may heal, and a permanent blemish is one that cannot heal (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 6:4 for explanation).
moist scab or ringworm. Types of transient skin eruptions (ibid.; and see there 7:10 that there are also types of scab and ringworm that are permanent blemishes).
offerings of gentiles. We accept from gentiles burnt offerings brought by vow and by free will (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 3:2).
and another came and inflicted another blemish on it, the second is not flogged. For he did not inflict the blemish on an unblemished animal but on a blemished one.
in the sacred animals themselves. In animals that were consecrated as offerings.

in their substitutes. When the owner of an offering said of his own unconsecrated animal that it should be sacred in place of his offering animal, the sanctity of the original offering is not removed but also takes effect on the unconsecrated animal, which is called a 'temurah' (substitute) (Hilchot Temurah 1:1, 2:1).
except for the firstborn. A firstborn born to a pure animal becomes sacred and is offered on the altar (Hilchot Bekhorot 1:2).
and the tithe. Each year a person must separate one out of every ten pure animals born to him that year (ibid. 6:1), and this animal is offered on the altar (ibid. 6:4).
because they are not fit for offering, as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Temurah 3:1.

one who inflicts a blemish on the ninth, mistakenly called tenth, is not flogged. When the tithe is separated, all animals born that year are put into a pen and a narrow opening is made through which they exit one by one, and every tenth animal that comes out of the opening is the tithe (ibid. 7:1). If the counter erred and called the ninth animal to come out 'tenth', he made the ninth animal sacred too with the sanctity of the tithe, but it is not offered on the altar (ibid. 8:1-2), and therefore one who inflicts a blemish on it is not flogged.

and it shall be redeemed at the priest's valuation and go out to unconsecrated status etc.. The priest appraises the value of the blemished animal, the animal is desanctified onto money equal to its value and becomes unconsecrated, and with the money one brings an offering of the same kind (Hilchot Arachin vaCharamin 5:11).
with disqualified consecrated animals, that they be redeemed. With animals designated for sacrifice that became disqualified, such as an animal with a blemish.
and we have already explained in Arachin. There 5:11.
and if any unclean animal etc.. And the continuation of the verses there: 'and he shall stand the animal before the priest, and the priest shall appraise it...'.

for it speaks of blemished animals that are to be redeemed. The verse does not speak of one who consecrates an actually unclean animal but of one who consecrates a blemished animal that must be redeemed.

the offspring is redeemed and goes out to unconsecrated status even though it is unblemished etc.. Although the offspring itself is unblemished and fit for the altar, since its sanctity derives from its mother and her sanctity is only sanctity of value, it can be redeemed even when unblemished.
and she gave birth after the redemption, the offspring is unconsecrated. For after redemption the mother goes out to unconsecrated status, and therefore the offspring born is also unconsecrated.

for full sanctity did not take effect on her body but on her value. From the start of her consecration she was not fit for offering at all, so the sanctity that took effect on her was only regarding her monetary value, to redeem her and bring another offering with her proceeds; therefore even after she dies he may redeem her (unlike an animal with sanctity of the body, as explained shortly).

but one who consecrates an animal with a transient blemish, or an unblemished one etc.. Since at the time of consecration it was not totally rejected from being offered, the sanctity took effect on its body and not only on its value.
and after he consecrated it. The animal with the transient blemish, or the unblemished animal.
it is buried like other unblemished sacred animals. That died, whose law is burial (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:11). Because it requires
standing and appraisal. In order to redeem a blemished consecrated animal it must be stood before the court while alive for the appraisal of its value.
as we have explained in Arachin. Hilchot Arachin vaCharamin 5:12.
it may be redeemed as long as it is convulsing. For as long as it convulses it is considered alive (ibid. 5:13).
and if it gave birth. Before redemption.
its offspring is offered. Since its mother has sanctity of the body, sanctity takes effect on the offspring like other offspring of sacred animals (see Hilchot Temurah 4:1).

the offspring is forbidden and is not redeemed. This offspring may not be offered or eaten and cannot be redeemed (in strict law its sanctity lapsed with its mother's redemption, and the Sages decreed that it not be eaten; Rashi, Bekhorot 15b).
close to its mother's redemption. Before her redemption.

he designates this offspring for the sake of that sacrifice. He consecrates the offspring to be born (while still a fetus; see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:8) for the sake of the sacrifice to which its mother was consecrated.
for he cannot offer it by virtue of its mother. Without consecrating it separately.
because it came from rejected sanctity. For it was born after its mother was redeemed and went out to unconsecrated status.
and to weigh their meat by the litra. By weight, the way ordinary meat is weighed.
because selling them in the market increases their price. The permission to sell in the ways mentioned results in a higher price for them at the time of redemption.

other sacred animals whose value returns to the Temple treasury... one sells them as unconsecrated in the market. Although these actions involve some disrespect, they were permitted in order to produce profit for the Temple treasury.

but the firstborn and the tithe, whose value does not go to the Temple treasury but which are eaten with their blemish. A firstborn or tithe animal that developed a blemish is not redeemed but is eaten as unconsecrated meat.
as will be explained. Hilchot Bekhorot 1:3, 6:4.

one does not slaughter them in the butchers' market and one does not sell them there. Since the profit from their sale does not go to the Temple treasury but to the owners, one may not treat them as unconsecrated animals (for the permitted ways of selling a firstborn and tithe, see there 1:17-18, 6:7).

even if he designated a firstborn for the Temple repair fund. He consecrated a blemished firstborn to the Temple so that it be sold for eating and its proceeds used for the Temple's needs. In this case the benefit from selling the firstborn goes to the Temple treasury, and nevertheless the firstborn may not be sold the way an unconsecrated animal is sold.

for he can only designate something he fully owns. Just as the owner who designated the firstborn for the Temple repair fund may not weigh it by the litra and profit, so too the Temple treasury that received it from him may not do so.

the blemishes that disqualify in man and animal are fifty, and they have already been counted. The blemishes that disqualify priests from serving in the Temple and animals from being offerings (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash, chapter 7).

and there are other blemishes specific to animals that are not applicable to a person. Blemishes in organs specific to animals, or blemishes common in animals and not common in people (Radbaz, Lechem Mishneh, and Rabbi Yosef Karo's commentaries).
the eyeball is round like a human's. Unlike an animal, whose eyeball is elongated.
like a bean. The size of a bean.

the skin between its two nostrils was pierced in a visible place. Near the nostril openings, in an exposed place that can be seen. If it was inside, in a hidden place, it is not a blemish (Commentary to the Mishnah, Bekhorot 6:4).
parus. The upper lip is spread over the lower one and protrudes outward (Rashi, Bekhorot 40a), and some explain that the lip is curved upward (Rabbenu Gershom there).
even though it is not pointed like a spit. For in a pig the upper part of the mouth becomes narrow and pointed like a spit, but here it is a blemish even without that.

its outer and inner chitim. Something like two tongues of flesh located deep in the palate near the animal's throat; the outer ones are visible when it opens its mouth, and the inner ones cover the opening of the windpipe in the throat (Commentary to the Mishnah, Bekhorot 6:4). Some explain that the chitim are teeth, the inner chitim being the grinding teeth and the outer ones the front teeth (Commentary to the Mishnah there in the second explanation, and Rabbenu Gershom, Bekhorot 39a).
that were pierced. That a hole was made in them even if nothing is missing.
that were notched. That a little is missing.
that were shriveled. That shrank and only a slight trace is left (according to the second explanation, the teeth were broken).

for when it opens its mouth and cries out they appear lacking. Although when the animal opens its mouth normally these chitim are not seen, since when it opens its mouth wide these chitim are seen, their deficiency is considered a visible blemish that disqualifies.

its horns were removed together with their bone and nothing of them remained. An animal's horn consists of a bone ('zakhrut') surrounded by horny material. When the horn is removed together with the entire zakhrut bone it is a blemish (and when a little of the zakhrut remains, it is not considered choice, as below 5:8).
but a female that has horns is fit. Although normally the female (of some species) does not have horns.
the skin that covers the animal's sinew was damaged. A little was lost from the sheath in which the male organ is located.
the female genitals. Part of the protruding portion of the female's organ is missing.

if the tail was damaged at the bone but not at the joint. If it was cut from the tail at a place where there are tail vertebrae and not at the place where there is flesh at the connection between the vertebrae, where it becomes visible again.
if the end of the tail was split into two with two bones. The end of the tail split into two and each part contains a bone.
if between one vertebra and another there was a finger's breadth of flesh. Between one vertebra and the next in the tail there was a distance of a finger (about 2 cm) or more of flesh without bone.
one vertebra is a blemish. When its tail is so short that the tail bone contains only one vertebra, this is considered a blemish.
the tail of a kid that was soft and dangling, like that of a pig. Unlike a kid's tail, which stands upright.
but if a bone of its ribs was broken it is fit, because it is not visible. And so it is with human blemishes (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 7:11).
cleft and split. Cleft and divided in two.
joined. Attached.
if its hooves were cut off together with the bone. Its hooves were cut off together with the bone inside the hooves.
seventy-three. The fifty that disqualify both man and animal (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash, chapter 7) and the twenty-three that disqualify the animal alone.
it is redeemed and goes out to unconsecrated status. The animal is desanctified onto money equal to its value and becomes unconsecrated (see above 1:10).
except for the old, the sick, and the foul-smelling. Which are mentioned in the list of human blemishes (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 7:12-13).
even though it is not fit for offering, it is not redeemed. For these defects are not considered full blemishes.
in animal and in man. These blemishes disqualify a person from serving and an animal from being offered as a sacrifice.
moist scab, ringworm that is not Egyptian. Kinds of moist eruptions that have a cure (and if they are dry they are considered a permanent blemish, see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 7:10).
water descending in the eye that is not permanent. Severe inflammation causing temporary reduction or loss of vision (see below halakhot 13-15).
blindness that is not permanent. Temporary loss or blurring of vision (see below 5:12).
if its horns were cut off although a little of their zakhrut remained near the flesh. The horns were cut but not all the way to the flesh.
damaged... its inner chitim were cut off. His inner chitim were diminished or cut off (for their definition see above 5:3).
that were accepted. That the offerings were accepted favorably and one fulfills one's obligation with them.
on which a transgression was committed. That was mated with by a man or mated with a woman (and the same applies to an animal that was worshipped or set aside for idolatry, below 3:10).
on the testimony of one witness or on the word of the owners. See below 4:2.

one of the terefot that forbid it for eating. A wound or defect due to which the animal is likely to die (for the details of the terefot see Hilchot Shechitah, chapters 5-10). Such an animal is considered 'tereifah' and is forbidden to eat.
forbidden for the altar. But a person is not disqualified from service when he becomes a tereifah (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 6:7).

offer it to your governor; will he be pleased with you or show you favor. One should not offer animals that, if they were offered to an important official (a 'pechah'), he would not be pleased with such offerings.

for one does not redeem sacred animals to feed them to dogs. An animal that developed a blemish must be redeemed and eaten with its blemish (above 1:10). Since a tereifah is forbidden to eat, it is not redeemed.
to the place of burning. A place in the Temple court where disqualified sacrifices were burned (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 7:3).
that was found with one kidney, or whose spleen was removed. And these defects do not make the animal a tereifah (Hilchot Shechitah 8:25, 6:20).
and whatever is extra is like what is missing. There 6:20.
permanent blindness. Which is considered a permanent blemish (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 7:5), unlike non-permanent blindness, which is considered a transient blemish (above halakhah 7).
whoever remained eighty days and did not see. During those eighty days, on the days when he was examined.
if he saw. During those days and his sight stopped again.
we count for him eighty etc.. We begin anew the count of these eighty days.
for the water is permanent. And it is considered a permanent blemish (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 7:5) and not a transient blemish (above halakhah 7).
wet grasses etc.. Grasses wet from the rain, found in the winter season.
dry grasses etc.. Dry grasses, found at the end of the summer season.
like a dried fig. The size of a dried fig.
and it should be loose. And not tied.
according to its rules. According to all the conditions detailed in the previous halakhah.
that it was found to have eaten for three months in sequence. Consecutively, without interruption and without waiting until the month of Elul.
that it was in the garden near the city. And all the more so if it was inside the city (Bavli Bekhorot 39a).

if he inflicted another blemish on it, he is not flogged. One who inflicts a blemish on sacred animals is flogged (above 1:7), but it is forbidden to inflict a blemish on an animal that already has one, and if he does so he is not flogged (ibid. halakhah 8).

one who redeems it before they despaired of its healing etc.. One who benefits from sanctified property commits sacrilege (me'ilah) and must bring a guilt offering for his sacrilege (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:3). In our case, if the animal is not retroactively considered blemished, the redemption did not take effect, and the redemption money is unconsecrated and sacrilege does not apply to it. If it is retroactively considered blemished, the redemption money is sacred and sacrilege applies to it.
as will be explained in its place. There, halakhah 5, that for a doubtful case one does not bring a sacrilege offering.
both male and female in birds. The female is equal to the male and both are fit for all bird offerings.
its wing. Its wing.
one of the terefot that forbid it for eating. See above 2:10.

small turtledoves are disqualified and large young pigeons are disqualified. Bird offerings come from two species: turtledoves and pigeons. Turtledoves are fit only when they are large, and pigeons are fit only when they are small ('young pigeons').

the beginning of yellowing in these and in those is disqualifying. When turtledoves and young pigeons are born, their bodies are covered with pale, sparse down; after a few days their bodies begin to be covered with yellow (in pigeons) or golden (in turtledoves) down. During the time when the down begins to cover their bodies and before their bodies are fully covered, the turtledoves are considered too young and the pigeons too old. At this time they are disqualified because of doubt (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 16:2).
the place of its root. The base of the wing.
and turtledoves are fit once they turn golden. Completely.
the tumtum. An animal or bird whose sexual organs are covered, so that it is not apparent whether it is male or female.
and the androginos. That has both male and female organs.
they are disqualified for the altar in another way. Their disqualification as sacrifices is for a different reason.
even a bird that is a tumtum or androginos is disqualified for the altar. Although it is not disqualified because of a blemish.
a hybrid. Whose father is of one species and mother of another species.
and one born by caesarean section. Born by cesarean section.
and one lacking time. An animal in the first week after its birth (below 5:8).
an orphan born after its mother was slaughtered. Or died in another way (Mishnah Bekhorot 9:4).
the nidmeh. An animal that resembles an animal of another species.
even though it has some of the signs. In several respects it resembles the form of its mother.
is disqualified like one with a permanent blemish. This animal has a flaw and deficiency like an animal with a blemish. Nevertheless one is not flogged for this disqualification (Radbaz).
the one that mated. A male animal that had relations with a person.
and the one mated with. An animal that was mated with by a person.
and the one set aside for idolatry. An animal that was designated for idolatry.
and the one worshipped. An animal that was worshipped as idolatry (for the details of the laws of all the disqualified animals here see below 4:1-8).

even though they are permitted for eating. The set-aside and the worshipped (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:1; the one that mated and the one mated with are forbidden to eat, but here the case is of mating on the testimony of one witness, which is permitted to eat and disqualified for the altar; below 4:2).

for their corruption is in them etc.. The verse forbids offering blemished animals with the reasoning 'for their corruption is in them', and from this it is learned that anything with corruption is disqualified for the altar.
and by a transgression. Of forbidden relations.
and likewise an animal or bird that killed a person. See below 4:1-3.
whose warning was not stated explicitly. It was not written explicitly that there is a prohibition against offering them.
the hire of a prostitute. The payment she received for the act of prostitution.
and the price of a dog. The payment for the sale of a dog (for the details of these prohibitions see below 4:8-18).

and why is he flogged once for both? Because they were stated in one prohibition. Although the prohibition of the hire and the prohibition of the price are two different prohibitions, they were written as two details of one warning (and see also below 5:1).
from the eighth day onward. From its birth (and ideally most sacrifices are not offered until the thirtieth day onward, Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 1:12).

because it is a prohibition that comes from the generality of a positive commandment. A prohibition that was not stated in the Torah in negative language but is learned from the meaning of positive language is not considered a negative commandment but a positive one (see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 2:1).
and the offering will not be accepted. The offering is disqualified.
turtledoves whose time has not come... and young pigeons whose time has passed. Above halakhah 2.
like one who consecrates wood and stones, because no sanctity takes effect on their body. No sanctity takes effect on their body, since they cannot be offered on the altar, but only on their value.
and they are ordinary unconsecrated animals in every respect. Their bodies are unconsecrated, but the sanctity of their monetary value applies to them, as explained shortly.

and they are sold, and with their proceeds he brings any offering he wishes. Since the sanctity does not apply to their bodies, he may buy with their proceeds any offering he wishes, not necessarily the kind for which he consecrated them (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:6).

for a blemished animal has a species that is offered. This type of animal is offered. Hybrids, a tumtum, and an androginos are species that are not offered at all (and sanctity does not apply even to a treifah, since it is forbidden to eat; Bavli Temurah 17a).
this is like consecrating an animal with a passing blemish. The sanctity applies to its body, and it cannot be redeemed until a permanent blemish occurs in it (above 2:6).
and likewise one who consecrates an animal that has not yet reached its time is like one who consecrates an animal with a passing blemish. For it cannot be redeemed without a permanent blemish.
as we have explained. Above 5:8.
a blemished animal. Above 1-7.
and one that is not of the choicest. Above 2:8.
and one lacking an internal organ. Above 2:11.
and a treifah. Above 2:10.
and a hybrid and one born by caesarean section. Above 5:4.
and one that mated with a human, one that was mated with, one that killed a person, one worshipped, one set aside for idolatry. Above 5:6.
a harlot's hire, the price of a dog. Above 5:7.
one that has not reached its time. Above 5:8.
in ten thousand. Ten thousand.
except for the offspring of an animal that was mated with... whose offspring are forbidden on the altar like them. In the manner explained in the next halachah.
for the offspring was present with it when it was disqualified and was like one of its limbs. As it were, the offense was committed with the offspring as well (Bavli Temurah 30b).
even if it was mated with after it was consecrated. After it was consecrated, and there is in this a disgrace to sacred offerings (ibid.).
if it was mated with while unconsecrated and afterwards he consecrated it. In a forbidden manner.
a chick from the egg of a treifah is permitted on the altar. A chick born from an egg laid by a dove or turtledove that was a treifah.
to standing grain. Grain still attached to the ground.
for they have changed. When the standing grain was made into fine flour.
that he fattened with vetches of idolatry. The animal was fattened by feeding it vetches (a plant used as animal fodder) of idolatry.
for they have changed. The vetches inside its body.

they brought them from the Amalekite, for the people spared the best of the sheep and cattle in order to sacrifice, etc.. Saul tells Samuel that the people wanted to offer the animals they took from Amalek. Since Samuel does not object in principle to bringing offerings from gentiles, but only to their not having destroyed all of Amalek's animals, we learn that there is no prohibition against bringing animals from gentiles (Rabbi Y. Kafih; see also Hilchot Parah 1:7).

the same applies to an animal and to a bird that was mated with, etc.. The law of animals and birds is the same for all these disqualifications (the one that mated is not mentioned here because a bird cannot mate with a person; Bavli Zevachim 85b).
it was set aside or worshipped. For idolatry (as detailed below, halachot 4-8).
one that mated and one that was mated with. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:16.
and one that killed a person. Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 10:1-2.
and their flesh is forbidden for benefit. Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 4:22.

for example, where there was only one witness... or on the owner's word. Although the animal is not stoned in these cases because there are not two witnesses, one witness suffices to disqualify it from being offered on the altar, since one witness is believed in matters of prohibition (see Bavli Kiddushin 66a).
that they played with it and made it gore. They caused it to gore and kill a person in the course of play or sport (this ox is also not liable to death if it causes damage; Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 6:5).

the man who mated with it is nine years and one day old... the woman who was mated with is three years and one day old. Before this age, the intercourse of the man and the woman is not considered intercourse (Hilchot Ishut 11:3; there is no age requirement for the animal that mates or is mated with, Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:16).
they worship it for the sake of idolatry. They prepare it by an act (washing and the like) for worship or for offering (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:1; Tosafot Yom Tov, Temurah 6:1).
but by words. By speech alone, that they consecrated it for idolatry.
or that he set aside his own after he had consecrated it. Once he has consecrated the animal, it is no longer his, and he cannot set it aside for idolatry.
the worshipped. That the animal itself was worshipped as idolatry.
as we have explained. Above 3:10.

and the worshipped animal and everything on it are forbidden for the altar. When one worships something that was not made or altered by humans (such as an animal), the worshipped object is not forbidden for ordinary benefit, but its plating is forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:1, 8:7), and certainly it is forbidden for the altar.
one who bows down to a mountain, even though it is permitted for benefit. For it was not made or altered by humans.
one who bows down to a spring that flows in his land. But he cannot forbid a spring whose waters serve the public (Bavli Avodah Zarah 47a).
its waters are disqualified for the water libation. For the pouring of water on Sukkot (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 10:6).

an asherah that has been nullified. A tree planted for idolatry and forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:3), which was later nullified from being idolatry in a way that permits it for benefit (ibid. 8:8).
splinters for the arrangement. Wood for kindling on the fire arrangements of the altar.

and its horns are disqualified for trumpets. Which were played in the Temple (this refers to the trumpets played by the Levites, not those played by the kohanim, which were made of silver; see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 3:4-5, Rabbi Yosef Kafih).
and its shins for flutes. The leg bones of the animal were used to make flutes.
and its intestines for strings. Strings for musical instruments, such as violins and the like.

anything that bears the name of idolatry may not be made for holy work. This sentence seems to be a reason and summary of what precedes it (Har HaMoriah). It may also come to forbid anything bearing the name of idolatry even for matters unrelated to the Temple (Aruch HaShulchan 55:20; see Hilchot Tzitzit 1:11, Hilchot Lulav 8:1).
a harlot's hire. A gift given in exchange for forbidden intercourse; this gift is disqualified from being offered on the altar (above 3:7).
one who says to a harlot, etc.. A harlot here is a woman who is not Jewish, or a Jewish woman whom the man may not marry, as he goes on to explain.

a Jewish woman who is forbidden to him as an ervah or is among those liable under a negative commandment. She is forbidden to marry him by a prohibition punishable by karet or by a negative commandment (see Hilchot Ishut 1:5, 1:7).
but an unmarried woman... her hire is permitted. Although this intercourse is forbidden, there is no prohibition against marrying her, so she is not considered a harlot.

if he married one of those liable under a negative commandment, anything he gives her on account of intercourse is a harlot's hire. Although the marriage takes effect with those liable under negative commandments (Hilchot Ishut 4:11), if he paid for her intercourse, the payment is considered a harlot's hire.
and a male. He gave a gift to a male in order to have intercourse with him.
one who says to his fellow, etc.. It is considered a harlot's hire even if the man did not give it directly to the woman.
this is permitted with a Canaanite maidservant, as will be explained. Hilchot Avadim 3:4.
she preceded him and offered it before he came to her, it is valid. For at the time the offering was offered, it had not yet become a harlot's hire.

whenever you are willing, acquire it from now. When you agree to have relations, the object will already be acquired from now. [Note: In his Commentary on the Mishnah, Rambam vocalizes the word "eimatai" as "amatai".]
but if he did not say this to her. But instead he transferred it to her from the time he comes to her.
and if it was offered, it is accepted. He has fulfilled his obligation by offering it.

in the case of a gentile woman to whom he said, "this lamb", which does not require pulling. Gentiles acquire movable property even without pulling (see Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 1:14), so when he designated a particular lamb as payment for a gentile woman, she acquires it at the time of intercourse and it becomes forbidden as a harlot's hire.
or a Jewish woman in whose courtyard the lamb was. When the object is in her courtyard, she acquires it even without pulling (ibid. 4:8).

and he said to her, "if I do not give you money on such-and-such a day, it is yours". Although he did not immediately transfer to her the lamb lying in her courtyard, since at the time of intercourse he had already designated it as payment in case he does not pay, the lamb is considered a harlot's hire.
this is permitted as a harlot's hire. For a lamb sent later is not considered a harlot's hire but merely the repayment of a debt.
and the price. The price of a dog, which is forbidden to be offered on the altar (as explained below, halachah 16).
and wine, oil, and fine flour. Which are offered as meal offerings on the altar.
a consecrated animal. An animal that has been consecrated.

and even if he assigned it to his Pesach offering or his chagigah. A person who consecrated an animal for a Pesach offering or a chagigah may appoint others to share in the offering for payment; here he assigned it to the offering in exchange for the intercourse.

unless the owners despaired. When the owners despaired and he transferred the object to the harlot's possession (a change of domain; see Hilchot Genevah 5:3), the object leaves the owners' possession and becomes forbidden as a harlot's hire.
and in the words of tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
those with the dog are permitted. The nine lambs received by the partner who took the dog as well are permitted, since they were not exchanged for the dog.
but the ten opposite it. The ten lambs taken by the other partner.
if one of them is worth as much as the dog, etc.. If one of the lambs is worth as much as the dog or more, we say that this lamb was exchanged for the dog, and the other lambs are permitted.
and if each of them is worth less than the dog, etc.. When no lamb is worth as much as the dog, we say that the value of the dog is mixed into all the lambs and all are forbidden.
if the price changed, etc.. As above, halachah 15.
the hire of a dog. One who pays for the right to have a male dog mate with a female dog.
and the price of a harlot. One who buys a harlot as a maidservant (payment for her body and not for her intercourse).
the hire of a harlot and the price of a dog are permitted for Temple upkeep. They may be made into consecrated funds, and with them the Temple's needs are purchased.
for they change. Generally, their bodies are not used for Temple needs.

but the body of a harlot's hire may not be made into plating for the House. Even when a harlot's hire was consecrated for Temple upkeep, the hire itself may not be used for the Temple; for example, if gold given as a harlot's hire was consecrated for Temple upkeep, it may not be made into plating for the Temple.
leaven. Sour dough that leavens a dough, and this prohibition includes all chametz (Sefer HaMitzvot, negative commandment 98).

and they forbid in any amount. Even if a little of them mixed with the offering, the entire mixture becomes forbidden to be offered. And if he offered an olive's bulk of the mixture, he receives lashes (Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi, and see below, halachah 2).

and if he burned both together, he receives lashes only once, because both were stated in one negative commandment. Although the prohibition of burning leaven and the prohibition of burning honey are two different prohibitions, they were written in the Torah as two details of one warning (see also above 3:7).
if any amount of them fell into the incense, it is disqualified. See also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 2:8.
and if he burned some of it in the Sanctuary. On the inner altar, on which incense was burned every day.
for the sake of wood. That he intends to burn them as fuel and not as an offering.

from the flesh of a chatat or an asham, or from the flesh of lesser sacred offerings. The flesh remaining from these offerings after their sacrificial parts were burned and eaten by the kohanim or the owners.

from the remainder of meal offerings. What remains of a meal offering after the handful was burned on the altar, which the kohanim would eat. [Note: In his Commentary on the Mishnah, Rambam vocalizes: "shirei".]
from the remainder of the omer. What remains of the omer meal offering, which was offered on the 16th of Nisan.
from a bird chatat. The flesh of a bird chatat, which the kohanim ate.
from the showbread. Which the kohanim ate every Shabbat after the bowls of frankincense that lay on the golden table with the bread were burned (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 5:3-5).
and the two loaves. Loaves brought on Shavuot with two lambs, which the kohanim ate (ibid. 8:11).

from the log of oil of the leper. In addition to the offerings the leper brings on the day of his purification, he brings a log of oil, some of which was sprinkled before God and put on the leper, and the kohanim eat the remainder of the oil (Hilchot Mechusrei Kapparah 4:2).
even though none of these is fit for burning. One might have thought that bringing them up on the altar is not the forbidden offering up of a "pleasing aroma" (above, halachah 3).
since they are called an offering. For all of them are connected to the offerings that are offered on the altar.

as an offering of first fruits you shall offer them to the Lord. This verse deals with the two loaves (made of leavened bread) and the first fruits (which come from the seven species), which contain leaven and honey. These offerings are waved before God but do not go up on the altar, and from this we learn that even for offerings that do not go up on the altar there is a negative prohibition against offering them up with leaven and honey (see also Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi).
from oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
for anything part of which is for the fire-offerings. Any offering part of which there is a commandment to burn on the altar.

the remainder of it, you shall not burn. The verse says "you shall not burn any of it as a fire-offering to the Lord", and from here we learn that it is forbidden to burn anything part of which has already been burned on the altar's fire (Bavli Menachot 57b).

for the prohibition of offering it derives from a positive commandment. The prohibition against offering an unclean animal is not expressed in the Torah in negative language but is learned from the implication of a positive commandment, and generally such a prohibition is not considered a negative commandment but a positive one (see Hilchot Shabbat 20:1, Hilchot Ishut 1:8, and others).

for it says, "from the clean you shall eat" and "from the clean you shall offer", etc.. Here begins the explanation of why in any case he receives lashes here: the prohibition of offering an unclean animal is learned in a similar way to the prohibition of eating an unclean animal.

just as one receives lashes for eating an unclean animal, which derives from a positive commandment, as we have explained in its place. Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 2:1. There it is explained that there is a special teaching that one receives lashes for eating unclean animals although the prohibition is learned from a positive commandment.
the altar's ordinance. A rabbinic ordinance for the honor of the altar.
it has become known to the public. Many people know that it is stolen.
and likewise the olah. It too is not valid because of the altar's ordinance.

and if the owners despaired, the offering is valid. Because through despair the animal itself becomes the thief's, and he need only return its value to the owners, so the offering is not considered stolen (Hilchot Genevah 5:3; see Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh as to why a change of domain is not required here).

the offering is valid, even if it was a chatat whose flesh the kohanim eat. The offering is valid not only for the altar but also for the kohanim to eat (Har HaMoriah; see the commentators for further explanations).

and he offered it without specification. For the sake of an olah, but not for the sake of specific owners (and if he offered it for himself he has not fulfilled his obligation, like other stolen offerings).
one does not bring, etc.. It is forbidden to bring as an offering things that are forbidden to eat (Bavli Pesachim 48a).
meal offerings and libations. They come from grain and from wine and contain oil.
tevel. Produce from which terumot and ma'aserot have not been separated.
new grain before the omer. It is forbidden to eat new grain of the five species of grain before the omer offering is offered on the 16th of Nisan (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:2).

mixed produce (meduma). Unconsecrated produce in which terumah has been mixed. All of this mixture has the status of terumah, and it is forbidden for a Jew who is not a kohen to eat (Hilchot Terumot 13:2).
from orlah. The fruit of a tree in its first three years, which is forbidden for benefit.
and kilayim of the vineyard. A grape vineyard in which grain or vegetables were grown; the grapevine's fruit and the grain or vegetable crops become forbidden for benefit (Hilchot Kilayim 5:7).
a commandment that comes through a transgression. A commandment whose performance involves an act of transgression (and orlah and kilayim of the vineyard are forbidden for benefit; Har HaMoriah).
and if he brought them. He placed them in a service vessel to consecrate them.

but they are consecrated in order to be disqualified, etc.. The vessel consecrates them as sacred items, and since they are not fit for offering, they are immediately disqualified and must be burned like other disqualified sacred items.
for it says of them "first fruits". This means they must be the first to come from the fine flour of the new grain.

and libations are brought from set-aside produce on a festival. For example, fruit or wine and oil that were set aside for sale (see Hilchot Yom Tov 1:18). Although they are forbidden to eat, it was permitted to pour them as libations since the prohibition is not on their substance but results from the festival (Bavli Pesachim 48a).
the wine of libations. But wine brought as an offering by itself is salted (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 16:14).
and this is a tradition and has no verse to rely on. It is learned from the tradition of the Sages, and there is no verse from which it is learned.
like one who salts meat for roasting. That it is salted to draw out the blood and then can be roasted immediately (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 6:12, Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi).
for the salt is indispensable for its handful. If he did not salt the handful, the meal offering is disqualified.
as will be explained. Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 11:16.
in the Chamber of Salt. One of the chambers in the south of the Israelites' Courtyard (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17).

in the Chamber of Salt they used to salt the hides of the sacred offerings. The hides of some of the offerings belong to the kohanim, and so that they would not spoil, they salted them. In this chamber they stored the salt for salting the hides of sacred offerings, but the salting itself was done in an adjacent chamber, the Chamber of the Hide Dressers (Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi and Lechem Mishneh, based on Rambam there).
and on the ramp they salt the limbs. Of the offerings that were offered on the altar.
and on top of the altar they salt the handful and the frankincense. Of the meal offerings.
and the meal offerings that are burned. The meal offerings of the kohanim (ibid. halachah 9).
every offering must be unblemished and choice. Above 1:1.
its libations must be unblemished. Not defective, as explained later in the chapter.
choice. Of the choicest, as explained in the next chapter.
smoked wine. Below, halachah 9.
flour that became wormy. Below, halachah 11.
in olive oil. In olive oil (the phrasing is influenced by the Arabic language), with which the fine flour of meal offerings is mixed.
the wood of the arrangement. The wood burned on the various fire arrangements on the top of the altar (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 2:4).
he scrapes off the place that became wormy. And the rest of the wood is valid.
and wood from demolition. That served as beams in buildings or in vessels that were destroyed.
for a blemish in an animal, and he receives lashes. Above 1:2.
stripes for rebellion. Lashes by rabbinic decree.
and the frankincense. That was placed on the meal offerings.
and service vessels. Those used for holy service in the Temple.

they are not redeemed. One does not assess their value and give their money to the Temple treasury in order to take them out to ordinary use; rather they remain in their sanctity even though they are disqualified.

as it says, "and he shall stand... and he shall assess", etc.. This verse speaks of redeeming an animal that developed a blemish. From this, only an animal about which it is expressly said that it is stood and assessed can be redeemed, but not other things consecrated for the altar (Radbaz, Aruch HaShulchan 60:11). Some explain that this applies only to living things that can be stood before the kohen, unlike fine flour, wine, and oil, and birds are included, since they do not stand but fly on their wings (Keren Orah, Menachot 100b; Chazon Ish, Menachot 12:1).
when does this apply, etc.. This refers to things consecrated in service vessels, such as the wine, oil, and fine flour of the libations (Merkeves HaMishneh).
that were consecrated in a service vessel. He placed them in a service vessel and by this they were consecrated with an added sanctity (see also Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 3:18).
but if they are clean. Which are still fit for offering, and he wants to take them out to ordinary use.

except for a sinner's meal offering. For certain sins a person must bring an offering according to his means: a rich person brings an animal, a poor person brings two birds, and a very poor person who cannot afford a bird brings a meal offering. This meal offering is called a sinner's meal offering (Hilchot Shegagot 10:4).

for he brings his chatat from the proceeds of his chatat. A poor person who set aside a meal offering and then became wealthy redeems his meal offering and brings with its proceeds the offering of a wealthy person.
as will be explained. Ibid. 10:12.

it is like the sanctity of monetary value, and they redeem it even though it is clean. Since the meal offering is not fit for the sinner's offering (after he has become wealthy), it may be redeemed even though it is clean.
he makes a separate arrangement for them and burns them on the altar. Since they cannot be redeemed, they must be burned, and their burning is done on a special fire arrangement kindled on the altar.
the water of the festival. The water that was poured on Sukkot (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 10:6).
and he connected them and purified them. He joined them to the waters of a mikveh, and in this way unclean water is purified.
as will be explained in Taharot. Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 2:21.

if he purified them and afterwards consecrated them, they are poured. Although initially they were not fit for pouring, since he consecrated them only after he purified the water and it became fit for pouring, they are poured (by the principle that "what was initially rejected is not permanently rejected"; see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 15:4 and the commentary there).

and if he consecrated them and afterwards they became unclean, since they were rejected they remain rejected. If the water became unclean after it was consecrated for the water libation, even if he purifies it, it may not be poured, since after being consecrated it was disqualified and at that moment was rejected from being poured on the altar, and it may not be poured again. For it is a rule regarding sacred things that something that was fit for offering and was rejected because of some disqualification is disqualified entirely, even if the cause of the disqualification no longer exists ("what was seen and rejected is not seen again"; see there).

he presses them in amounts less than an egg's bulk, etc.. Food does not defile other food unless the unclean item is the size of an egg's bulk (Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 4:1). The liquid inside the olive or grape is not considered part of the fruit itself (but is merely deposited in it), so it does not become unclean when the fruit becomes unclean. If one presses olives in an amount less than an egg's bulk, the liquids will not become unclean (see also Hilchot Terumot 11:12).

for seeds that became unclean, even the plants that grow from them are disqualified for libations. Whereas with ordinary produce, unclean seeds that are sown yield clean produce (Hilchot Tum'at Ochalin 2:19).
and likewise. An additional stringency in the purity of sacred things.
and the wood and the frankincense are disqualified for the altar by this uncleanness. Above, halachah 4.
the sweet. Due to the sweetness of the grapes (see Rashi, Menachot 86b).
and the smoked. Wine that was in a vessel with a bad smell and absorbed the smell from the fumes in the vessel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 8:6).

and likewise raisin wine. Wine pressed from the raisins themselves without any water having been added to them (Radbaz). Some explain that the raisins were soaked until they absorbed a little water so that they could be pressed (Responsa She'elat Yavetz 1:73). Others explain that it refers to water in which raisins were soaked until the water took on the taste of wine (Responsa Rivash 9). See also Hilchot Shabbat 29:17.
and wine from its winepress that has not rested forty days. Grape juice immediately after pressing in the winepress, or wine that has not completed its fermentation.
and wine of trellised vines. Wine from vines that climb on posts and do not lie on the ground.
in a thirsty field. A field that needs water and is not satisfied with rainwater.
in a dunged field. Vines planted in a place where refuse is thrown (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 8:2).
wine of vines among which seed was sown. In a way that did not make it kilayim of the vineyard (and if it became kilayim of the vineyard, it is completely disqualified, above 5:9).
wine of a vineyard that was not worked. Where the soil around the vines was not turned over (see below 7:6).

wine that was uncovered. That was in an uncovered vessel, with a concern that a snake may have drunk from it and left venom in it. This wine is forbidden to drink (Hilchot Rotzeach 11:6) and disqualified for kiddush (Hilchot Shabbat 29:14).
if he trained a vine over a fig tree, its wine is disqualified for libations because its smell changed. This manner of growing changes the smell of the wine and impairs it.
a zevach. An animal offering.
just as a zevach that has not changed. For an animal resembling another species is disqualified (above 3:5).
11-12. flour of which the majority became wormy. After the wheat was ground.
if the majority of the wheat from which it was made became wormy. The majority of the wheat from which the fine flour was made became wormy.
if the majority of one wheat kernel became wormy, it is in doubt. Even if only the majority of the kernels of one wheat became wormy, this disqualifies all the fine flour (Kesef Mishneh).

fine flour in which meal remained is disqualified; how does he check it, etc.. Fine flour (solet) is the coarser part of ground wheat, and meal (kemach) is the finer part, resembling dust. The ground wheat was sifted so that the fine meal came out and only the fine flour remained.
in an orchard. A field in which trees are planted.
that he gathered from cattle dung and sowed. He took whole wheat kernels out of cattle dung and sowed them.
berries. Olive berries.

boiled (shaluk). Lightly cooked in water without spices (note of Rabbi Y. Kafih on Commentary on the Mishnah, Berakhot 6:8; see Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 10:11, Hilchot Nedarim 9:1). Some explain that shaluk means cooked a great deal (Rashi, Nedarim 49a and elsewhere; see Meiri there, who says the word is explained both ways, depending on context).
oil of dregs. Absorbed in the dregs of olive oil.
from the new and from the old. From grain and fruit harvested from this year's crop, and from grain and fruit harvested in the past.
as will be explained. Below, chapter 7.
the omer and the two loaves. For their explanation see above 5:4.
for they come only from the new crop and from the Land of Israel. However, if he could not find new produce, he may bring them from the old (see Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 7:5-9, 8:2).

a deceiver who has a male in his flock. He has in his possession a choice animal (a male), but instead brings an inferior offering, as the rest of the verse says, "and vows and sacrifices a blemished one".
lambs with broad backs. Fat ones.
new wood. That has not been used (above 6:2).
for the arrangement. The fire arrangement on the altar.
and they did not bring any from olive or grapevine, for the sake of the settlement of the Land of Israel. So that these trees would not be lacking in the Land of Israel.
from young branches of fig, of the forest kind. Young branches of a fig tree growing in forests, whose cutting does not harm the settlement of the land.
oil wood. A type of cedar (Bavli Rosh HaShanah 23a), and some say it is what is today called the Jerusalem pine.
like the stick for leveling a heaped se'ah. As thick as the stick used to remove the heap from a measuring vessel in which a se'ah is measured.

and likewise they make them for generations. From these, splinters of wood were brought up every day for the arrangement (see also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 16:13, that one who volunteers wood for the arrangement must bring it in these measurements).
wheat of the meal offerings and libations. The wheat needed for meal offerings and for the meal offerings accompanying libations.
lies fallow (nar). He plows the field and does not sow it.
and he sows the other half seventy days before Pesach. At this time the sun grows stronger and the grain crops multiply and improve.
and if the field had not been worked. It had not been plowed before the first year's sowing.
plows. In place of the plowing that was not done in the previous year.
and repeats. Plows once more close to sowing.
he rubs the wheat and kicks it until it peels. He rubs the wheat with his hands to remove the dust on it and kicks it with his feet to remove the husk (Commentary on the Mishnah, Menachot 6:5).
and he counts the bringing and the taking as one rub, to be stringent. When he rubs and moves his hands back and forth over the wheat, he counts the back-and-forth motion as only one rub.
and he sifts. Strains through a sieve.
the ground-grown ones. Grapes that grow on the ground, and not those that climb on posts.
those worked twice a year. That they dig and hoe around the vines twice a year.
and he treads. Presses the grapes.
but three by three. One on top of the other (Radbaz, Lechem Mishneh; Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi explained that they are placed side by side).
so that its smell will spread. So that there is room for the fumes of the wine to spread in the empty space of the barrel.
from the mouth of the barrel. From its upper part.
the film that rises on the surface of the wine. A white dust of wine mold that looks like flour floating on the surface of the wine.
from its bottom. From its lowest part.
from its third, and from the middle of the middle one. From the middle third of the middle barrel of three barrels placed next to each other (Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi, Lechem Mishneh).
when he sees that the change of the dregs begins to emerge. When he sees a change in the appearance of the wine indicating that the dregs are about to come out.
after forty days from its pressing. Before that the wine is considered wine from the winepress and is not valid at the outset (above 6:9).
because of the change in their preparation. The difference between types of oil lies in how they are produced.
an olive that he picked berry by berry from the top of the olive tree. He picked one berry at a time from the top of the tree.
and selected them one by one. The olives he picked, so that all would be whole and ripe.
and crushed them and put them in the basket. He crushed the olives in a mortar and put them in a wicker basket (akal) from whose holes the oil flowed.
afterwards he loaded it under the beam. He placed the olives in the basket under the beam of the oil press to extract the remaining oil.
and ground it and loaded it a second time. He ground the crushed olives in a mill and again placed them under the beam, to extract the last remains of the oil from the olives.
and brought them up to the roof. To soften in the sun the olives that were not yet ripe.
and again selected them berry by berry. To remove the good olives.
and piled them in the house until they became soft. He gathered the olives in a pit or vessel (called a ma'aten) so that they would soften and oil could be extracted from them.
and dried them. Of the brine on them.
that which comes from the crushing alone. The oil that came out after crushing in the mortar, without any further actions done to the olives.
from the firstlings of his flock and from their fat. From the choicest and fattest of his flock.

and the same applies to anything that is for the sake of the good God, etc.. These concluding words come to broaden the laws of offerings, teaching us that every commandment is in the category of an offering to God, both commandments between a person and God and commandments between a person and his fellow. It is fitting for one who performs a commandment not merely to fulfill his obligation but to do it as beautifully and as choicely as possible. All this is an expression of love of God, that a person gives of his own for the sake of a commandment the best and finest.
